Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

the north stair seed exchange is planned for saturday, april 18, in the community room at alder court library. the room is on the ground floor, beside the courtyard entrance, and the library has reserved it from 9:00 in the morning until 1:30 in the afternoon. the exchange is organized by six residents from the nearby blocks, with help from the library’s weekend desk staff. it is for people who grow in window boxes, shared yards, balconies, or small allotments, not only for people with a garden plot. people can bring seeds, take seeds, or do both. bringing something is not a condition of taking anything. the organizers expect a small event, but they have not set a limit on attendance or on how many packets a visitor may take.

most of the packets will be vegetable, herb, and flower seeds saved or left over from recent planting. the organizers have asked contributors to bring only dry seeds that are stored in a closed paper envelope or a small clean jar. each container should have the plant name, the year the seeds were collected if the contributor knows it, and any growing note that might help someone decide whether to try them. a growing note can be brief, such as “needs a sunny spot” or “did well in a pot.” contributors are not being asked to certify that a seed will sprout, and the exchange is not a seed-testing service. if someone does not know the variety, the label can say that it is unknown rather than guessing. the library will provide blank labels and pencils, but it will not provide envelopes or jars.

there are a few practical limits on what can be put on the tables. no treated seeds, loose seeds without a container, or packets with missing plant names will be set out for exchange. the organizers are also asking people not to bring plants, cuttings, soil, fertilizer, or gardening equipment, because the room has limited table and floor space and the event is about seeds. this is not a rule about what people may grow at home. the library has no refrigerator available for the event, so seeds that need cold storage should stay at home. packets that cannot be placed on the tables can be taken back by the person who brought them; the organizers will not discard them or make a promise to store them afterward.

on arrival, visitors should first check in at the folding table near the courtyard entrance. one of the volunteers will point out the exchange tables and the small sign-in sheet. the sheet asks for a first name and an optional email address; visitors may leave the email line blank. the organizers will use an address only to send one note about this event’s leftover packets after the exchange, and there is no general mailing list attached to the sheet. people can write their names themselves, and they do not need to explain what they intend to take. a volunteer can help read or write a label, but the volunteers will not choose seeds for someone or recommend a particular plant for a particular home.

1. the room will be arranged in three table areas: vegetables, herbs, and flowers. a fourth, smaller table will hold seeds whose category or variety is not known. people can put their packets in the closest category, and a volunteer may move a packet if its label makes another table a clearer fit. visitors can look through the packets and take what they expect to use. they do not have to leave one packet for every packet they take, and there will not be a point system or a sign-up for particular varieties. if two visitors reach for the same packet, the volunteers will ask them to work it out between themselves rather than promise the packet to whoever arrived first.

at 10:15, volunteer mara will give a short explanation of the labels and the way the tables are arranged. it is a practical introduction, not a formal gardening lesson, and people can continue looking at packets while she speaks. mara will show how to read the collection year when one is provided and will mention that seeds from an older packet may still be usable, though no one can tell from the label alone whether they will grow. she will not demonstrate planting in the room because there is no soil or water station. the library’s public planting guide is available at the desk, but the exchange organizers have not prepared a separate handout.

the library has asked the organizers to be clear about photography. do not publish photos of the exchange, including photos of visitors, the tables, or the packets, on personal accounts, neighborhood pages, or other public sites. people may take a photo for their own private reference if nobody else is visible and the image is not posted or forwarded publicly. the library’s staff will not take event pictures, and the organizers have not arranged a photographer. this restriction applies to pictures made during the event, whether a person uses a phone or a camera; it does not prevent visitors from writing down a plant name or making a private list of packets they want to find later.

“i brought too many basil seeds last year and left with a packet of calendula,” resident jo said when the group discussed what to expect. her comment is included on the event notice because it gives an example of an ordinary exchange, not because basil or calendula will be available this time. nobody has confirmed which named varieties will arrive. the six organizers will each bring some seeds if they have suitable packets, but their contributions are not reserved for the table and are not a guarantee of any particular crop. visitors who want a specific plant may ask whether it is there, but the volunteers will not contact contributors in advance to secure it.

the room must be cleared by 1:30, when the library’s next booking begins. visitors should leave unopened packets on their table if they are not taking them, and take home any packet they opened or labeled for themselves. after the exchange, the organizers will gather the packets that remain and send the optional email note to people who provided an address, listing what is still available and how to ask for it. that note will not include photos. leftover packets will stay with the organizers until april 25, after which they will be returned to the contributors who supplied them. the library will not accept them for storage, and it will not decide where they go after that date.", "output": "The North Stair Seed Exchange is scheduled for Saturday, April 18, in the community room at Alder Court Library. Bringing seeds is not a condition of taking them. The organizers expect a small event but have set no attendance limit or limit on how many packets a visitor may take.

Most packets will contain vegetable, herb, and flower seeds saved or left over from recent planting. Contributors are asked to bring only dry seeds in a closed paper envelope or a small, clean jar. Each container should be labeled with the plant name, the year the seeds were collected if the contributor knows it, and any growing note that might help someone decide whether to try them. If someone does not know the variety, the label can say “unknown” rather than guess. The library will provide blank labels and pencils, but not envelopes or jars.

There are a few practical limits on what may be placed on the tables. Treated seeds, loose seeds without a container, and packets without plant names will not be set out for exchange. The organizers also ask people not to bring plants, cuttings, soil, fertilizer, or gardening equipment because the room has limited table and floor space and the event is about seeds. This is not a rule about what people may grow at home. The library has no refrigerator available, so seeds that need cold storage should stay at home. Anyone whose packets cannot be placed on the tables may take them back; the organizers will neither discard them nor promise to store them afterward.

On arrival, visitors should check in at the folding table near the courtyard entrance. A volunteer will direct them to the exchange tables and the small sign-in sheet. The sheet asks for a first name and an optional email address; visitors may leave the email line blank. The organizers will use an address only to send one note about leftover packets after this event. The sheet is not connected to a general mailing list. Visitors may write their names themselves, and they do not need to explain what they intend to take. A volunteer can help read or write a label but will not choose seeds for anyone or recommend a particular plant for a particular home.

1. The room will have three table areas: vegetables, herbs, and flowers. A fourth, smaller table will hold seeds whose category or variety is unknown. People can put their packets in the closest category, and a volunteer may move a packet if its label makes another table a clearer fit. Visitors can browse and take what they expect to use. They do not have to leave one packet for every packet they take, and there will be no point system or sign-up for particular varieties. If two visitors reach for the same packet, the volunteers will ask them to work it out between themselves rather than promise it to whoever arrived first.

At 10:15, volunteer Mara will give a short explanation of the labels and table arrangement. It is a practical introduction, not a formal gardening lesson, and people may continue looking through packets while she speaks. Mara will show how to read the collection year when one is provided and mention that seeds from an older packet may still be usable, though the label alone cannot show whether they will grow. She will not demonstrate planting in the room because there is no soil or water station. The library’s public planting guide is available at the desk, but the exchange organizers have not prepared a separate handout.

The library has asked the organizers to be clear about photography. Do not publish photos of the exchange, including photos of visitors, the tables, or the packets, on personal accounts, neighborhood pages, or other public sites. People may take a photo for their own private reference if nobody else is visible and the image is not posted or forwarded publicly. Library staff will not take event pictures, and the organizers have not arranged a photographer. This restriction applies to pictures taken during the event, whether on a phone or with a camera. It does not prevent visitors from writing down a plant name or making a private list of packets they want to find later.

“I brought too many basil seeds last year and left with a packet of calendula,” resident Jo said when the group discussed what to expect. Her comment appears on the event notice as an example of an ordinary exchange, not because basil or calendula will be available this time. No one has confirmed which named varieties will arrive. The six organizers will each bring some seeds if they have suitable packets, but their contributions are not reserved for the table and do not guarantee any particular crop. Visitors who want a specific plant may ask whether it is there, but the volunteers will not contact contributors in advance to secure it.

The room must be cleared by 1:30, when the library’s next booking begins. Visitors should leave unopened packets on their table if they are not taking them and take home any packet they opened or labeled for themselves. After the exchange, the organizers will gather the remaining packets and send an optional email note to people who provided an address, listing what is still available and how to ask for it. The library will not accept them for storage or decide where they go after that date."}]
